title: The Ledger of Merit and Demerit
author: Translated and annotated by Mingde
excerpt: The Ledger of Merit and Demerit is a register for those who refrain from evil and practice good, by which they spur and examine themselves. It has two parts: a merit grid (good deeds) and a demerit grid (evil deeds), one page a month, bound into a book. Day by day one records the merit or demerit of one's behavior, such as one merit, ten merits, a hundred merits, or one demerit, ten demerits, a hundred demerits. Only the number is recorded, not the deed, and it is entered separately into the merit grid or the demerit grid respectively.

inline.s: The Ledger of Merit and Demerit is a register by which those who refrain from evil and practice good spur themselves and examine themselves self-critically. It has two parts, the merit grid (good deeds) and the demerit grid (evil deeds), one page a month, bound into a book. Day by day one records the merit or demerit of one's behavior as good or evil, such as one merit, ten merits, a hundred merits, one demerit, ten demerits, a hundred demerits. Only the number is recorded, not the deed, and it is entered separately into the merit grid or the demerit grid. Each evening one settles the account; merit and demerit are offset against each other, and the remainder is the fixed merit or the fixed demerit. For example, if today one has ten merits and one demerit, then today's fixed merit is nine; if it is ten demerits and one merit, then today's fixed demerit is nine. Doing thus every day, at the end of the month one makes a small tally, accumulating the number of merits and demerits of the month, then offsets merit against demerit and carries the resulting merits or demerits over to the following month. At the end of the year, one again carries over the accumulated merits or demerits into the following year. Proceeding thus, one keeps clear measure in mind day by day, month by month, year by year, and practices diligently without ceasing.

blocks.text: The Ledger of Merit and Demerit (Original Text)

inline.s: Fei Ehu said: "The Ledger of Merit and Demerit is extremely precise and subtle, and men and women, rich and poor, may all practice it. Moreover it cultivates both deed and intention, and directly reaches those of superior capacity. Whoever receives this ledger records his merits and demerits each day on the calendar. One merit is marked
θ
, ten merits with ⊕, a hundred merits with ⊗; one demerit is marked
, ten demerits with ※, a hundred demerits with ⊛. One offsets the demerits against the merits, and the remainder is reckoned as the fixed tally. At the new and full moon
(the first and fifteenth of each month)
one burns incense and reports to Heaven, and dedicates the merit until one's good vows are fulfilled. Practicing diligently without ceasing, when one accumulates a hundred ⊗
(a hundred hundred-merits, that is, ten thousand merits)

, one may become a sage or worthy; gods and spirits hold one in reverence; whatever one vows is surely obtained, and no blessing fails to come. The ancients Fan Wenzheng, Su Meishan, and Zhang Weigong all received this ledger and reverently believed and practiced it. My honored father
(my father)
obtained it from the Tao family of Kuaiji, kept it in a treasure room as a night-light, and cherished and practiced it. He once dreamed that this ledger turned into gold characters, and so Hong
(Fei Ehu's own name, Fei Hong)
was born, and became a zhuangyuan; again he dreamed that the ledger turned into silver characters, and so the younger brother Cai was born, and became a jinshi. Only we humble brothers
(I and my younger brother Fei Cai)
deeply fear that we do not resemble
(do not resemble: a self-effacing expression, akin to 'unworthy')
, so morning and evening we reverently practice it, and therefore I make it public to those of like mind
(therefore I have made it public to those of like mind and shared aim)
[Fei Ehu (

)] His surname was Fei, his given name Hong, his courtesy name Zichong, his sobriquet Jianzhai, and also Ehu. He was a zhuangyuan of the Ming dynasty and a grand secretary of the Ming cabinet. Fei Hong was intelligent and fond of study from childhood; at
he placed first in the boy's examination of Xinzhou Prefecture (the wenyuan); at
he sat the provincial examination in Jiangxi and placed first (the jieyuan); at
he sat the palace examination and placed first among the jinshi (the zhuangyuan). In the ninth year of Zhengde

he served as Minister of Revenue. Because Fei Hong exposed the ambition of the then Prince Ning, Zhu Chenhao, to usurp the throne, he suffered persecution and resigned his office and returned home. (Note: Prince Ning Zhu Chenhao's power was very great; he plotted rebellion in Nanchang and sought to bribe Fei Hong with silk, coin, and rare treasures. Fei Hong refused, saying: "I hear that Prince Ning is carting gold to the capital to scheme the restoration of his guards. If one were to let him do as he pleases, we people of Jiangxi would surely be left without a single soul. (
jiào

kind, creatures that can eat, especially referring to the living; while I am in the cabinet one day, I will never permit this." He came under attack and was forced to resign.) In the sixteenth year of Zhengde

, the Shizong emperor succeeded to the throne and summoned Fei Hong back to court, where he succeeded as Minister of Personnel and was further ennobled as Corregent and Junior Preceptor, and concurrently Grand Preceptor to the Crown Prince. In the sixth year of Jiajing

, the remnant party of Prince Ning, unhappy at Fei Hong's elevation and ennoblement, continued to attack and frame him, forcing Fei Hong to return home once more. While at home, Fei Hong closed his gate in Yanshan, reading and writing, and did a great deal of charitable work for his hometown; he even opened the 'Hanzhu Academy,' engaging renowned teachers to lecture and instruct the members of his clan and the young of neighboring villages, and he himself taught for several months. In the fourteenth year of Jiajing

, the Shizong emperor once more brought Fei Hong, who had retired into the forest, back to serve as grand secretary of the cabinet. This was Fei Hong's third entry into the cabinet. In the tenth month of the same year
he passed away without illness, at the age of

. Fei Hong had the seasoned talent for benefiting the world. Though his official career went through twists and turns, he always maintained noble integrity and pure virtue, governing the realm together with Yang Tinghe, Yang Yiqing, and others, and was deeply relied upon by the ruler and his courtiers and praised by the common people. When the Shizong emperor heard of his death, remembering that Fei Hong had been loyal to the state and had served the four emperors Chenghua, Hongzhi, Zhengde, and Jiajing as a meritorious old minister, he conferred upon Fei Hong the title of Grand Guardian, suspended court for one day, personally composed three sacrificial eulogies, and led officials of the third rank and above to the Fei residence to mourn. He further sent the Grand Councilor Xia Yan to escort the coffin back to Fei Hong's hometown, and ordered burial according to the rites of a nine-thousand-year noble. Funerary works at Fei Hong's burial site were built under the charge of the Ministry of Works, including a memorial archway, ornamented pillars, stone men, stone horses, stone sheep, stone lions, and stone tigers; the grave tablet was engraved 'The Tomb of Fei Hong, Grand Light-Dispensing Grand Master, Pillar of the State, Junior Preceptor and Concurrently Grand Preceptor to the Crown Prince, Minister of Personnel, Grand Secretary of the Huagai Hall, Conferred Wenxian Duke.'

In one day one is sure to have more than ten merits to be cultivated; when accumulated to half a month, then over and above the merits of one's own grade one enters an additional ten merits; this prizes pure goodness. If in the midst there are one or two matters that do not meet the standard, then none may be entered separately. When urging one's own kin to goodness, a single great matter counts as ten merits; when it concerns an outsider it counts as only one merit — this honors kin and exalts filial piety and fraternal love. Ten merits in a day, and ten more entered at the half month, means a month may reach three hundred and twenty merits and a year four thousand merits. Such merit is extremely easy to accumulate and the recompense extremely swift. Yet one must be strict in self-reproach: even the most trivial demerit must be recorded, and one must not gloss over demerits while keeping full count of merits. All the accumulated merits are matters of daily, ordinary conduct that need no money, therefore poor men and women may all practice it. As for great perversity, wicked rebellion, killing, theft, the destruction of relationships, and a woman's wantonness and violence, her cruel slaughter of other living beings, and her jealousy that cuts off progeny — these are grave sins and extreme evils, and are not within the demerit limit. All within the grid are everyday household matters; as for great loyalty and great filial piety, great integrity and great righteousness, and the official who so benefits the people that a single deed may stand for ten thousand good acts — these likewise are not within the merit limit.
[Other-born beings]
an alternate name for the ordinary person, because the ordinary person revolves through the six realms and is born receiving all kinds of differing karmic retributions.

blocks.text: 5. The Grid of Persuasion and Transformation

inline.s: To transform through wordlessness, and to seek the worthy, is placed first; to transform heroes and the powerful and noble has double merit.

[To transform through wordlessness, and to seek the worthy, is placed first; to transform heroes and the powerful and noble has double merit] To transform people by one's own example, and to seek out the worthy, is placed first; to transform heroes and the powerful and noble has double merit (this is because heroes and the powerful and noble have great influence over society). [To transform through wordlessness] not to use verbal instruction but to transform by one's own example, imperceptibly changing people's minds and customs. The Record of the Four Lessons of Master Liaofan says: In the past Shun, on the shore of Leize Lake, saw that the young and strong fishermen all seized the deep pools and backwaters where fish were abundant, while the old and weak had to fish in the rushing shallows and could catch nothing. Shun's heart could not bear it, and he pitied these old and weak ones, so he too went fishing. Shun, seeing those who fought over the best spots, avoided speaking of their faults; seeing those who yielded, he praised and emulated them everywhere. After a year everyone yielded the deep pools and backwaters to one another. If Shun, with his brilliant wisdom, could not have lectured everyone with a set of reasons? The reason he did not use verbal instruction but transformed by his own example, imperceptibly changing people's minds and customs, is precisely the painstaking heart of a master craftsman!

blocks.text: 6. The Grid of Relief

inline.s: To rescue before [a calamity] occurs,

(if it reaches the point of being about to occur, there will surely be those who cannot be rescued in time. How much the more so once it has already occurred? Therefore the two words 'before it occurs' are subtle: the more hidden the virtue, the greater the merit!)
and to save the many through the art of benevolence

(as far as one's strength reaches, though it may pile up to hundreds and thousands, in the end there is a limit; only what the art of benevolence saves is without limit, and one who holds office governing the people should pay special attention)
, is placed first. Being skilled in medicine and skilled in swimming
(skilled at swimming)
, and rich merchants and those who travel far
(traveling far means encountering many situations; rich merchants possess the means; such people especially must arouse their intention, and the recompense is immeasurable)
, may all save people.

[Not yet occurred] something that has not yet become fact. [To rescue before it occurs] to rescue when disaster has not yet arisen. The idiom 'bending the chimney and moving the firewood' is exactly 'to rescue before it occurs.' [Bending the chimney and moving the firewood] A guest, seeing that the chimney of the master's stove was straight and that firewood was piled beside it, said to the master: "You should rebuild a bent chimney, lest the sparks keep flying out, and move the firewood to a distance. Otherwise, a fire might break out." The master fell silent and did not answer. Before long the house indeed caught fire, and the neighbors came together to fight the blaze, and fortunately they put it out. Then the master slaughtered an ox and set out wine to thank his neighbors. Those burned in the fire (their heads scalded and faces blistered) were seated in the places of honor, and the rest were seated in order by the size of their contribution, but the guest who had advised him to 'bend the chimney and move the firewood' was not invited. Then someone said to the master: "If back then you had listened to the guest's advice, you would not have suffered the fire, nor would you have gone to the expense of laying out a feast. Now when you appraise the merit and invite the guests, why is the one who advised 'bending the chimney and moving the firewood' not invited, while the burned are honored as the guests of honor?" Only then did the master awaken, and he hastened to invite that guest. [The art of benevolence] the policies, measures, methods, and techniques that benefit the people. For example: strategies of benevolent governance, medical skill, new-energy techniques, and so on. [One who holds office governing the people should pay special attention] officials especially should pay double attention. Because they administer the livelihood of the people, and practicing the art of benevolence can relieve very many people. The Record of the Four Lessons of Master Liaofan records that when Master Yuan Liaofan was county magistrate of Baodi, seeing that the people's burden was too heavy and their life miserable, he investigated the facts in detail, reported to his superiors, and memorialized the court, until the grain levy was reduced from two fen three li seven hao per mu to one fen four li six hao; this single item alone equaled ten thousand good deeds.

blocks.text: 7. The Grid of Dealing with Wealth

To cut off the root of private profit and advantage is placed first; the poor person who is not greedy is particularly meritorious.

inline.s: To constantly face and emulate them is placed first.

and praise. When a minister receives the ruler's gift, he often uses this word.
[To constantly face and emulate them is placed first] to constantly feel gratitude, praise, and emulate is placed first.
In one day, reverently serving the spirits and ancestors, or praying for the blessings of one's parents, seeking good conditions, and with utmost sincerity observing the fasts.
one merit
Repairing and setting up temples and sacred images, offering to the Buddha and feeding the monks.
one merit per hundred coins
Gathering written paper and burning it.
one merit per hundred characters
Constantly thinking of the sages, worthies, immortals, and Buddhas, keeping them solemnly in the mind, up to fifteen days.
ten merits

Up to awakening and sleeping with spiritual penetration, the luminous jewel-like appearance constantly flowing through the heart and lungs, as if wandering in the heavenly palace or hearing the speech of the gods. Expounding the teachings of the worthies and sages.
a hundred merits each
Profaning the scriptures. Making dirty written paper. Discharging
(urine and feces)
and spitting without regard to the three lights
(sun, moon, and stars)
. Praying for blessings and warding off calamity, yet not practicing good deeds, and vowing evil wishes with sacrificial animals. A woman fond of entering temples.
one demerit each
Mocking, insulting, and slandering the sages and worthies. Disrespecting the ancestors
ten demerits each
Striking and cursing the gods and spirits. Defiling temples. Advocating rebellion against the sages.
a hundred demerits each

[Gathering written paper and burning it] In ancient times, all paper bearing writing carried the words of the sages, so it had to be respected; it must not be defiled or discarded, but should be reverently burned. This is respect and cherishing for the words of the sages. [Warding off calamity] to dispel calamity.

blocks.text: 11. The Grid of Preserving the Mind

inline.s: To forget one's good deeds and to be free of self is placed first.
[Forgetting one's good deeds] not to store up the good one has done within the mind.
[Forgetting one's good deeds and being free of self]

The Record of the Four Lessons of Master Liaofan says: to use wealth to help people, without within seeing oneself, without without seeing the recipient, and in the middle not seeing the wealth given — this is the emptiness of the three wheels, this is single-minded purity. Doing thus, one dou of grain can plant immeasurable blessings, and a single coin can eradicate the offenses of a thousand kalpas. [The emptiness of the three wheels] the 'three wheels' are the giver, the recipient, and the thing given; after giving, not keeping these three wheels in the mind is called 'the emptiness of the three wheels.'
In the course of a single day, if one’s words and deeds are all good, one’s mind set on aiding the world and guiding the multitude,
one merit
and if for fifteen days one shares goodness with others and mends one’s faults day by day,
ten merits
and if for a whole month no selfish thought appears, one’s thoughts are few and dreams cease, and one’s intent grows ever more sincere,
a hundred merits
and if one is constantly thus, compassion natural, and holding to an empty, rounded responsiveness
(being utterly sincere)
and responding to all things
(the mind, without clinging, treating people and matters with fullness)
this is counted as immeasurable merit.
Lustful thoughts, greedy thoughts, evil thoughts, envious thoughts, thoughts of flattering the world, turning here and there
(tossing about)
are not removed.
one demerit
If evil thoughts turn and linger for several days and show themselves in one’s actions
ten demerits

[Sharing goodness with others]When doing good, inviting others to do it together; it also means: if one has a good point, wishing others to be like oneself, and if others have a strength, learning from them. [No selfish thought appearing, few thoughts and ceasing dreams, intent ever more sincere]When no selfish thought rises, one’s thoughts are few and dreams cease, and one’s intent grows ever more sincere. Kun
kun
: utterly sincere. [Turning here and there]Tossing and turning, unable to be at rest.
A verse in praise:
Without leaving the door, one saves ten thousand lives.”

(Giving timely help to insects and ants, and teaching one’s descendants to be of service to the world — educating one’s descendants to adulthood so as to save people. This is what is meant by ‘without leaving the door, one saves ten thousand lives.’)
Without spending wealth, one performs ten thousand merits.”

(Friendly and accommodating in filial and brotherly duties, which can be done on the spot; keeping patience and endurance in the mind — the merit is limitless. This is what is meant by ‘without spending wealth, one performs ten thousand merits.’)
Without relying on laws, one crosses over ten thousand people.”

(Praising good people, rejoicing in good deeds, publishing books of goodness, and stirring up thoughts of goodness. This is what is meant by ‘without relying on laws, one crosses over ten thousand people.’)
[Without relying on laws, one crosses over ten thousand people]Without depending on policy or statute, one is able to rescue and deliver thousands upon thousands of people.

blocks.text: The Ledger of Merit and Demerit (Vernacular)

rows.s: 4. The Category of Treating Subordinates with Leniency
5. The Category of Persuasion and Guidance
6. The Category of Relief and Rescue
7. The Category of Dealing in Wealth
8. The Category of Extravagance and Thrift

10. The Category of Revering the Sages
11. The Category of Guarding the Mind

inline.s: Mr. Feeh Lake said: the Ledger of Merit and Demerit is extremely subtle; men and women, rich and poor alike, can all practice it. Moreover, while cultivating good deeds in matters, one also cultivates good in intention, so that it can directly guide those of superior faculties. Whoever receives this ledger should each day note his merits and demerits on a calendar. One merit is recorded as
Theta
, ten merits as the circled-plus sign, a hundred merits as the circled-multiply sign; one demerit is recorded as
a cross
, ten demerits as an asterisk, a hundred demerits as the circled-asterisk sign. Offsetting merits against demerits, the surplus is the day’s fixed merit or fixed demerit.
(For example, if today one has ten merits and one demerit, then today’s fixed merit is nine; if ten demerits and one merit, then today’s fixed demerit is nine.)

On the first and fifteenth of each month one burns incense and tells Heaven, and having fulfilled one’s good vow, transfers the merit. Practicing thus unceasingly, when one accumulates a hundred hundred-merits
(ten thousand merits)

, one can become a sage or worthy; the spirits revere and admire one, whatever one vows is attained, and no blessing fails to come. The predecessors Fan Wen-cheng, Su Mei-shan, and Zhang Wei-gong all received this ledger, reverently believed, and practiced it. My father obtained it from the Tao family of Kuaiji; from then on this humble home was as if illumined by a night-shining pearl, and so he treasured it exceedingly and followed it. He once dreamed that this ledger turned into golden characters, and thereupon I
(Fei Hong)
was born and won first place in the palace examination; and again he dreamed that this ledger turned into silver characters, and my younger brother
(Fei Cai)
was born and passed the metropolitan examination. But we two brothers greatly feared that we were unworthy
(of becoming useful men)
, and so morning and evening we devoutly uphold it; now we specially make it public to those of like mind.
Note: Mr. Fei E-hu (

) was surnamed Fei, named Hong, styled Zi-chong, titled Jian-zhai, and also known as E-hu. A top scholar (zhuangyuan) of the Ming dynasty, he became the grand secretary of the Ming court (equivalent to a prime minister). From childhood Fei Hong was intelligent and fond of study;
he sat the children’s examination in Xinzhou Prefecture and placed first (wen-yuan);
he sat the provincial examination in Jiangxi and placed first (jie-yuan);
he sat the palace examination and placed first as a jinshi (zhuangyuan). In the Zhengde

th year he became Minister of Revenue. Because he exposed the ambition of Prince Zhu Chen-hao of Ning to seize the throne, he was persecuted and forced to resign and return home. (Note: Prince Zhu Chen-hao of Ning had great power and plotted rebellion in Nanchang; he sent Fei Hong gifts of silks and jewels, but Fei Hong refused, saying, “I hear the Prince of Ning carries his gold up to the capital, plotting to restore his guards; if we let him do as he likes, we people of Jiangxi will have none left alive [jiao-lei,
jiào
those creatures that can eat, that is, the living]. As long as I remain in the cabinet a single day, I will never allow it.” For this he was attacked and driven to resign.) In the Zhengde

th year, Emperor Shizong succeeded to the throne and recalled Fei Hong to court, appointing him Minister of Personnel and conferring on him the titles of state tutor to the heir-apparent and junior preceptor. In the Jiajing

th year, the remnants of the Prince of Ning’s faction, displeased at his advancement, renewed their attacks and slanders against him, forcing him to return home a second time. While in retirement he closed his door in Qianshan to read and write, and did many public works for his hometown, also opening the “Han-Zhu Academy”, engaging renowned teachers to lecture to his clansmen and the sons of neighboring villages, and himself teaching for several months. In the Jiajing
th year, Emperor Shizong recalled Fei Hong, then living in retirement, and made him grand secretary of the cabinet; this was his third entry into the cabinet. In the tenth month of that same year
he died without illness at the age of

. Fei Hong had the apt talent for benefitting the age. Though his official career was full of turns, he always upheld his lofty integrity, governing the empire together with Yang Ting-he and Yang Yi-qing, and was deeply relied upon by sovereign and courtiers alike and praised by the people. When Emperor Shizong heard the news, mindful that Fei Hong had served the state with a loyal heart through the four reigns of Chenghua, Hongzhi, Zhengde, and Jiajing as a meritorious elder, he conferred on him the title of Grand Guardian, suspended court for a day, and personally composed three funeral eulogies, leading officials of the third rank and above to the Fei household to pay their respects. He also sent the grand secretary Xia Yan to escort the coffin back to Fei Hong’s hometown and ordered a burial according to the rites of a nine-thousand-year lord. The works at his burial ground were constructed by the Ministry of Works, including memorial archways, ornamental pillars, stone figures, stone horses, stone sheep, stone lions, and stone tigers; his tombstone was inscribed “Bestowed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Pillar of the State, Junior Preceptor, Grand Guardian of the Heir-Apparent, Minister of Personnel, Grand Scholar of the Huagai Hall, Posthumously Conferred Duke Wen-xian, the Tomb of Fei Hong”.

If in each day one has more than ten merits, and accumulates them to half a month, then in addition to the merits of one’s own class one records ten extra merits, for this is precious wholly-good. If in the interval there are one or two matters that do not meet the standard, then one may not record the ten extra merits. As for urging one’s own relatives to do good, one major matter counts as ten merits; urging an outsider to do good counts as only one merit — for this is to value kindness to kin and to exalt filiality and brotherly love. If in one day one has ten merits, and at half a month one adds ten more, then in a month one may have three hundred twenty merits, and in a year four thousand. Thus accumulating goodness is very easy and the recompense very swift. Yet one must strictly reprove oneself; the least fault must be recorded, and one must not note merits in detail while noting demerits in a cursory way. The merits accumulated are all matters of daily and constant practice, costing no money, so the poor and women alike can practice them. Whatever is grossly contrary
(persons who greatly violate ethical principles)

, vicious, rebellious, murderous, thieving, the ruin of morals, and likewise a woman’s wantonness and raging, her cruelly killing the common folk, and her jealousy causing the extinction of an heir — these are crimes of the greatest evil and are not within the scope of the demerits spoken of in this ledger. The good and evil in this ledger are all ordinary household matters; whatever is great loyalty and great filiality, great integrity and great righteousness, and whatever an official does in bestowing great benefit upon the people, where a single act may count as ten thousand good deeds — these likewise are not within the scope of the merits spoken of in this ledger.

blocks.text: 1. The Category of Filial Piety

inline.s: To persuade and influence one’s parents and parents-in-law to cultivate the Way
(Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism)
is the foremost matter. For one able to be filial to a mother who is not one’s own, the merit is doubled.
In the course of a single day, serving parents and parents-in-law, toiling for them and bringing them joy, causing the hearts of parents and parents-in-law to be often glad.
one merit
Assisting in every good deed. Dissolving the anger of parents and parents-in-law, easing their anxieties.
each, one matter, one merit
Being filial to parents and parents-in-law for fifteen days, diligent and unwearied. Persuading parents and parents-in-law to reform a fault and move toward goodness in one great matter.
each, ten merits
Persuading and guiding
parents and parents-in-law to practice benevolence and perfect virtue.
a hundred merits
When father and mother are at odds, persuading them to reach harmony and joy.
one matter, a hundred merits
Toiling yet complaining. Proud yet lazy. Causing father and mother to become angry.
each, one demerit
Deceiving one’s parents for gain. Being disobedient and quarrelsome. Refusing to follow when taught what is good. Causing father and mother alarm and worry.
each, ten demerits
Obstructing the good of parents. Inciting parents to evil. Bringing danger and disgrace to parents. Long delaying the burial of an elder’s coffin
(when an elder has passed away, putting off the burial)
each, a hundred demerits

blocks.text: 2. The Category of Harmony

inline.s: To persuade and influence women to be loving and do good is the foremost matter; for a woman
(the case in which the person herself is a woman)
who can herself be at peace and do good, the merit is doubled.
In the course of a single day, among brothers, husband and wife, sisters-in-law, aunts, and maternal aunts, loving one another, sharing burdens, and yielding the easy
(yielding to others the light and pleasant tasks)
. Assisting in one good matter.
each, one merit
Being harmonious for fifteen days without weariness. Persuading one person to reform a fault and move toward goodness in one great matter.
each, ten merits
Transforming one person to practice benevolence and perfect virtue. When kindred
(brothers, husband and wife, sisters-in-law, aunts, and maternal aunts)
are at odds, persuading them to reach harmony and joy
each, a hundred merits
Not being affectionate and agreeable.
one demerit
Contentious and slanderous. Indulging wife and children while abandoning filiality and brotherly love.
one matter, ten demerits
Obstructing good. Praising evil. Being at odds all one’s life
A husband, through private favoritism, abandoning his wife; a wife trampling
(the same as ‘bullying’)
over her husband.
both, a hundred demerits

blocks.text: 3. The Category of Compassionate Teaching

inline.s: To teach one’s children from infancy to associate with good people is the foremost matter; and one able to teach in this way a child not one’s own, the merit is doubled.
Each day instructing descendants, nephews, and grandnephews, with kindness and even-handed love, neither angry nor indulgent. In great matters, after instruction they are able to obey.
each, one merit
In compassionate teaching for fifteen days without weariness, seeing them make progress. Obtaining worthy teachers and friends, and teaching them in goodness.
each, ten merits
Educating one person until he perfects virtue
(bringing his moral character to completion)
a hundred merits
Shielding one’s own children.
one demerit
Teaching children to strike and curse people and to take advantage. Approving the evil of one’s children.
both, ten demerits
Mishandling children who are not one’s own. Indulging descendants in evil habits.
both, a hundred demerits

blocks.text: 4. The Category of Treating Subordinates with Leniency

inline.s: To set one’s own body right and serve as a model to one’s subordinates
(maids, servants, and concubines)
in order to teach them is the foremost matter; and for a mistress
(the lady of the house)
able to enable a concubine to bear a child, the merit is doubled.

blocks.text: 5. The Category of Persuasion and Guidance

inline.s: To teach people by the example of one’s own body, and to seek out worthy men, is the foremost matter; in teaching heroes and the high and powerful, the merit is doubled
(because heroes and the powerful have great influence on society)
On a single day, concealing evil and proclaiming good, and often speaking of cause and effect and retribution to persuade people.
one merit
Persuading a person to do good and having him comply.
each matter, one merit
Printing and distributing scriptures and teachings, and preserving and benefiting the scriptures of nature and life
(and protecting the scriptures beneficial to one’s nature and life)
each hundred coins spent, one merit
In persuasion for fifteen days without weariness. Gaining one good person and with one heart transforming together. Settling and ending lawsuits.
each, ten merits

Persuading people to hold to ethics, and relatives to be at peace together. Transforming one person to benevolence and filiality. Persuading an evil person to reform his ways. Transforming a prodigal into a family man. Energetically preventing one great deed of harm to others. Publishing and writing supremely fine good works.
all, a hundred merits
Praising evil deeds. Exposing another’s private faults. Deceiving an ignorant person. Seeing a person’s evil and not remonstrating. Talking fondly of the pleasures of lust and gambling.
each, one demerit
Praising evil. Inciting lawsuits. Slandering a good person. Enticing a prodigal. Performing licentious plays. Inverting right and wrong.
each, ten demerits

Publishing and writing tales that injure morals. Enticing a good person to do evil. Breaking one person’s precepts and practice. Sowing discord among people’s own flesh and blood. Slandering a woman. Being a teacher instructing disciples without putting forth one’s whole heart. In a year of famine, egging on price-raising and compelling contributions.
each, a hundred demerits

blocks.text: 6. The Category of Relief and Rescue

inline.s: To rescue before disaster occurs
(to save a person before the calamity has come about,
for once the disaster has taken shape or even already arrived, it may be too late to save; so one must save as early as possible — the more hidden the virtue, the greater the merit!)
and to save the many by benevolent arts, is the foremost matter. Those skilled in medicine and skilled in swimming
(good at swimming)
, wealthy merchants and far travelers
(far travelers encounter much, and wealthy merchants have money; such people especially must arouse their vow, and their recompense is limitless)
— all these can save people.
[Benevolent arts]Policies, measures, methods, and techniques that benefit the people. For example: strategies of benevolent governance, medicine, and new energy technologies, and so on.
On a single day, rescuing whatever creatures one meets. Lending without stint. Hurrying with medicine to the sick. Curing a light illness by art. Lodging the homeless for a night.
each, one merit
Relieving hunger and cold and lack of goods.
one matter, one merit
Helping to build bridges and repair roads, providing ferries, digging wells, establishing public graves
(burial grounds for unclaimed bodies)
and pavilions, giving coffins, tea, and medicine.
each hundred coins, one merit

Relieving disasters and calamities. Aiding critical illness. Saving a grave illness by art. Curing the sickness of a wayfarer. Taking in the alone and unsupported. Saving one person from vagrancy. Giving land to bury an unclaimed body, and at the same time removing a harm to the people. Clearing one person’s wrongful charge
(clearing away one person’s injustice)
. Saving the life of a beast of a person able to repay one’s kindness.
each, ten merits

Throughout fifteen days striving to save and release one great beast or great fish or bird; if there is no great beast or great fish or bird, then reckoning it by middle or small creatures. A middle-sized one counts as a hundred, a small fish or small bird a thousand, or all the insects, shrimp, and snails
(for example, buying all the shrimp of a shrimp seller in order to release them)
ten merits

Saving the starving from death. Saving those who hang, drown, or take poison. Persuading people not to drown their children, or to have abortions, and having them comply. Finding means to rescue and raise abandoned children. Preserving a woman’s chastity. Establishing public granaries
(granaries set up against famine)
and free schools
(where poor children study free of charge)
. Advocating the repair of vital bridges and dangerous roads.
all, a hundred merits
Raising one undertaking whose benefit extends endlessly.
counted as immeasurable merit.
When one meets a disaster and is begged to save, being able to save and not saving. Seeing a wrong done and being able to right it and not righting it
(seeing a person wronged, being able to clear him and not clearing him)
. Killing insects. Mistreating animals. A woman privately making offerings to monks and Daoists.
each, one demerit

Breaking up one marriage. Casting away a corpse. Raping a woman who had already lost her chastity. Teaching people to fish and hunt. Advocating the killing of life. Suspecting illness and prescribing reckless medicine.
each, ten demerits

Causing a couple to be separated. Forcing people to wander and lose their homes. Depriving a woman of her chastity. Drowning and killing children. Teaching people to drown children and have abortions. Seeing creatures near death and, being able to save them, not saving them. Privately cooking cattle and dogs. Stealing and killing livestock.
each, a hundred demerits
Initiating one thing whose harm is endless.
this is counted as immeasurable demerit.

blocks.text: 7. The Category of Dealing in Wealth

inline.s: To root out the very foundation of “seeking private gain and taking advantage” is the foremost matter
(when a person acts against reason in matters of money, the root is seeking private gain and taking advantage, so to strike at the root is most effective)
, and the merit of one who is poor yet not greedy is especially great.
In the course of a single day, in transactions and sales, acting everywhere with generosity and leniency. Paying the government taxes early.
each, one merit
Lending money, taking pawns, and renting out fields, relieving people in danger and distress, without regard to interest.
one matter, one merit
Returning property that another has lost.
each hundred coins, one merit
For fifteen days benefitting others without weariness. Forgiving the debts of the poor. Leading the villagers to balance and standardize the measures of bushel and peck.
all, ten merits
Forgiving debts to save people from pawning their wives and selling their children, and matters touching life itself. Picking up precious treasure and returning it.
each, a hundred merits
Grinding down interest. Taking beyond what is right
(what is not one’s own due)
, taking a needle or a blade of grass without asking.
each, one demerit
Taking advantage of another’s urgency to take more. Relying on position to demand donations in the name of the public. Taking wealth by deceit. Accepting private benefit behind the backs of the many
(accepting private gain while turning from the public)
. Extravagantly spending the money of others
(wasting the wealth of others)
. Hiding property that another has lost.
each hundred coins, counted as one demerit
Pressing the destitute for debts. Conscience-stricken in owing money. Using two kinds of scales and measures. Mixing in false and counterfeit goods.
each, ten demerits
Slipping away from heavy debts
(unjustly avoiding repayment of a heavy debt)
. Scheming to ruin another’s property. Setting traps to lure people into gambling and dissipation. Making counterfeit silver, and using it knowing it to be counterfeit.
all, a hundred demerits
Borrowing a name to collect alms and enriching oneself.
a thousand coins, a hundred demerits

blocks.text: 8. The Category of Extravagance and Thrift

inline.s: To practice frugality on oneself while being able to give is the foremost matter; in wealth and honor not being dissolute, and women not contending for gaudy ornament, the merit is doubled.

In the course of a single day, in food and clothing rejoicing in simplicity and cherishing one’s blessings, and practicing giving and relief. The poor, peaceful in their labor, neither complaining nor greedy.
each, one merit

For fifteen days abstaining from cooking and killing, restraining appetites and desires, men at their trades and women at their work, not wasting food and clothing. Transforming one person to be not extravagant or licentious. A whole household frugal and given to giving.
each, ten merits

blocks.text: 9. The Category of Nature and Conduct

inline.s: To transform one’s temperament by enduring loss and humiliation is the foremost matter; one should at all times advance and amend.
[Temperament]The quality of one’s mind and character.

In the course of a single day, respecting the old and cherishing the young, loving and being kind to one’s fellows, enduring humiliation and bearing toil, treating noble and base alike, repaying kindnesses and dissolving grievances. Hearing words that grate on the ear. Receiving an affront without anger. Being slandered without defending oneself
each, one merit
For fifteen days without weariness, transforming one quality of temperament. In a great matter, enduring what is hard to endure.
each, ten merits
Anger never arising, rejoicing everywhere, transforming everywhere.
a hundred merits

Arrogant and contumelious. Jesting with sharp and cutting words. Evil speech and cursing. Making a nickname to mock someone. Fabricating songs and ballads. Sowing discord between people. Failing a promise. Stealing another’s excellence.
According to the size of the matter; if great, the fault is tenfold.
Empty words to buy favor
(speaking falsehood to ingratiate oneself)
. Women fond of idle wandering. Much talk and foul abuse.
each, one demerit
Delighting to speak of women. Encroaching on the weak and deceiving the foolish. Using cunning to scheme secretly
(using schemes to plot in secret)
. Fabricating slander to defame and frame a person. Destroying another’s success.
all, ten demerits
Getting practiced in quarreling, litigation, and aggression. Using sorcery to harm people. Setting the heart on injuring others. A woman bewitching and dominating her husband.
all, a hundred demerits
[Two tongues]Stirring up right and wrong and driving a wedge between people.

blocks.text: 10. The Category of Revering the Sages

inline.s: To constantly give thanks, praise, and emulate is the foremost matter.
Profaning the scriptures. Making filth of paper with writing on it. Passing
(urine and feces)
and spitting without regard for the Three Lights
(the sun, moon, and stars)
. When praying for blessings and warding off calamity, not cultivating goodness but making the evil vow to sacrifice livestock. Women fond of entering temples and monasteries.
each, one demerit
Mocking and slandering sages and worthies. Showing disrespect to one’s ancestors
each, ten demerits
Striking and cursing the gods. Defiling and damaging monasteries. Advocating rebellion against the sages.
all, a hundred demerits

blocks.text: 11. The Category of Guarding the Mind

inline.s: In the course of a single day, if one’s words and deeds are all good, one’s mind set on aiding the world and guiding the multitude,
one merit
and if for fifteen days one shares goodness with others and mends one’s faults day by day,
ten merits
and if for a whole month no selfish thought appears, one’s thoughts are few and dreams cease, and one’s intent grows ever more sincere,
a hundred merits
and if one is constantly thus, compassion natural,
(being utterly sincere)
and holding to an empty, rounded responsiveness
(the mind, without clinging, treating people and matters with fullness)
this is counted as immeasurable merit.
Lustful thoughts, greedy thoughts, evil thoughts, envious thoughts, thoughts of flattering the world, turning here and there, are not removed.
one demerit
If evil thoughts turn and linger for several days and show themselves in one’s actions
ten demerits
